title: Quiz · Nervous System
section: 1. How is the Nervous System different from Hands?
text:
1. How is the Nervous System different from Hands?






TipShow answer





Hands change an external system: one capability, one target, one action. A Nervous System senses, communicates, and coordinates across many participants: many messages, event-driven, many-to-many. They share the same posture (provider-neutral, identity-bound, adapter-backed) but solve different problems.

title: Quiz · Nervous System
section: 2. Name the semantic message types the transport carries and what each one means.
text:
2. Name the semantic message types the transport carries and what each one means.






TipShow answer






observation — something is observed (sensor data, telemetry).
event — something happened (a state transition others may react to).
command — a request to perform an action on a specific target.
delegation — a Pico asks another Pico to carry out a mission.
result — the outcome of a command, delegation, or mission.
presence — a Pico is reachable on the transport right now.

title: Quiz · Nervous System
section: 3. Why is the Pico Agent Transport provider-neutral, and where does EMQX/MQTT fit?
text:
3. Why is the Pico Agent Transport provider-neutral, and where does EMQX/MQTT fit?






TipShow answer





So that Picos depend on stable message semantics rather than a specific broker or protocol. EMQX/MQTT is a candidate implementation / adapter of the transport — one of several possible implementations (alongside A2A, in-process buses, and future transports). Replacing the transport means swapping the adapter, not rewriting Pico rules or messages.

title: Quiz · Nervous System
section: 4. Why must Pico identity be independent of MQTT client IDs, broker sessions, and hostnames?
text:
4. Why must Pico identity be independent of MQTT client IDs, broker sessions, and hostnames?






TipShow answer





Infrastructure identifiers may change on every reconnect, scale operation, or Pod rescheduling. Pico identity must not. Binding authorization, evidence, or memory to an infrastructure identifier would break as soon as the infrastructure changed and would let two different Picos accidentally share an identity across reconnects.

title: Quiz · Nervous System
section: 5. What does “a valid broker session must not imply authorization” mean?
text:
5. What does “a valid broker session must not imply authorization” mean?






TipShow answer





Broker authentication answers “is this client permitted to open this connection and publish to this topic?” That is a transport concern. Open Engineering authorization answers “is this Pico permitted to observe, command, or delegate this capability in this context?” Being allowed to publish to a topic does not automatically permit the capability the topic represents.

title: Quiz · Nervous System
section: 6. Why is discovery treated as a first-class Pico capability rather than a broker feature?
text:
6. Why is discovery treated as a first-class Pico capability rather than a broker feature?






TipShow answer





A Pico should be able to determine which peers exist, which are currently available (presence), what capabilities they advertise, and under what constraints — without hard-coding a peer list and without depending on a specific broker’s discovery extension. The transport carries discovery messages; Open Engineering owns the meaning of “this Pico advertises capability X.”

title: Quiz · Nervous System
section: 7. Why does an incoming message not automatically become long-term memory?
text:
7. Why does an incoming message not automatically become long-term memory?






TipShow answer





Delivery is a communication concern. Classification and retention are cognitive concerns owned by the Pico’s rules and memory. The Pico decides whether each message is transient, an observation, an event, a mission input, or evidence. Collapsing delivery and memory would either flood the Pico with noise or lose evidence that must be retained.

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
In this lab you will author one artefact per semantic concern of the Nervous System — discovery, presence, observation, event, command, delegation, result, authorization, and memory classification — and validate every artefact as local YAML.
The scenario is a small two-Pico interaction that mirrors the runtime Hello Two Picos lab without requiring a running cluster:

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Setup
mkdir -p scratch/nervous

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 1 — Discovery advertisement
Create scratch/nervous/discovery.yaml. This is what a Pico advertises about itself to the transport, provider-neutrally.
# scratch/nervous/discovery.yaml
pico:
  identity:
    id: pico-alice
  kind: garden-detective
  capabilities:
    - garden.moisture.read
    - garden.watering.request
  protocols:
    - pico-agent-transport      # provider-neutral
  status:
    state: online

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 2 — Presence
Create scratch/nervous/presence.yaml. Presence is a distinct message type from discovery: discovery is what a Pico offers, presence is whether it is reachable right now.
# scratch/nervous/presence.yaml
message:
  type: presence
  source: pico-alice
  timestamp: 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
  payload:
    state: online

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 3 — Observation
Create scratch/nervous/observation.yaml. Observations are sensor-shaped data; they are not events until a Pico interprets them.
# scratch/nervous/observation.yaml
message:
  type: observation
  source: pico-alice
  subject: garden/soil
  timestamp: 2026-01-01T00:00:01Z
  payload:
    moisture: 32
    unit: percent

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 4 — Event
Create scratch/nervous/event.yaml. An event is a state transition other participants may react to.
# scratch/nervous/event.yaml
message:
  type: event
  source: pico-alice
  subject: garden/soil/dry
  timestamp: 2026-01-01T00:00:02Z
  payload:
    threshold: 40
    observed: 32

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 5 — Command
Create scratch/nervous/command.yaml. A command names a capability on a target, never a broker topic.
# scratch/nervous/command.yaml
message:
  type: command
  source: pico-alice
  target: pico-bob
  subject: garden.watering.request     # provider-neutral capability
  correlation: cmd-001
  payload:
    duration_s: 60

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 6 — Delegation and Result
Create scratch/nervous/delegation.yaml and scratch/nervous/result.yaml. A delegation is a mission handed to another Pico; the result closes it via the same correlation value.
# scratch/nervous/delegation.yaml
message:
  type: delegation
  source: pico-alice
  target: pico-bob
  subject: mission.investigate_dry_zone
  correlation: mission-001
# scratch/nervous/result.yaml
message:
  type: result
  source: pico-bob
  subject: mission.investigate_dry_zone
  correlation: mission-001
  payload:
    status: completed
    evidence-reference: memory/evidence.yaml

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
section: Step 7 — Authorization decision (identity, not client ID)
text:
Step 7 — Authorization decision (identity, not client ID)
Create scratch/nervous/authorization.yaml. Keep transport authentication and Open Engineering authorization as separate keys.
# scratch/nervous/authorization.yaml
transport_authentication:
  broker_session_ok: true            # Transport concern only
  broker_client_id: "must-not-be-treated-as-identity"
open_engineering_authorization:
  actor: pico-alice                  # stable Pico identity
  capability: garden.watering.request
  target: pico-bob
  decision: allow
  bound_by:
    - rule: rules/allow-watering.yaml#0

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 8 — Memory classification
Create scratch/nervous/memory.yaml. Not every delivered message becomes long-term memory; the Pico classifies each one.
# scratch/nervous/memory.yaml
classifications:
  - message: observation.yaml
    classification: transient          # discarded after evaluation
  - message: event.yaml
    classification: observe            # short-lived working state
  - message: delegation.yaml
    classification: mission            # kept for the duration of the mission
  - message: result.yaml
    classification: evidence           # retained as verifiable memory

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 9 — Validate all nine artefacts
Every file is local YAML. No broker is used. These are Nervous System governance and message artefacts, not Hello Pico Rules, so the check uses python3 to confirm each file is well-formed YAML with the expected shape. pico parse only accepts the flat Rule shape (id/kind/value) taught in Part 1.
python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, yaml, pathlib
root = pathlib.Path("scratch/nervous")
names = ("discovery","presence","observation","event","command",
        "delegation","result","authorization","memory")
required_types = {"presence","observation","event","command","delegation","result"}
seen_types = set()
failed = False
for name in names:
    path = root / f"{name}.yaml"
    try:
        doc = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text())
    except yaml.YAMLError as exc:
        print(f"FAIL: {path} — {exc}", file=sys.stderr); failed = True; continue
    if not isinstance(doc, dict) or not doc:
        print(f"FAIL: {path} — expected a non-empty YAML mapping", file=sys.stderr)
        failed = True; continue
    if "message" in doc and isinstance(doc["message"], dict):
        seen_types.add(doc["message"].get("type"))
    print(f"OK: {name}.yaml parses")
missing = required_types - seen_types
if missing:
    print(f"FAIL: missing semantic message types: {sorted(missing)}", file=sys.stderr)
    failed = True
sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)
PY

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
section: Step 10 — Optional annex · MQTT/EMQX topic mapping (non-runnable)
text:
Step 10 — Optional annex · MQTT/EMQX topic mapping (non-runnable)






WarningOptional and non-runnable in this wave



This annex illustrates how a semantic Nervous System message could be carried by MQTT/EMQX. It is not executed, no broker is contacted, and it is not a prerequisite for completing the lab. No credentials, tokens, or EMQX account are needed.


# scratch/nervous/mqtt-mapping.yaml   (illustrative only — do not run)
transport: mqtt
mappings:
  event:        picos/{source}/event/{subject}          # QoS 1, retained: false
  observation:  picos/{source}/observation/{subject}    # QoS 0
  command:      picos/{target}/command/{subject}        # QoS 1
  delegation:   picos/{target}/mission/{subject}        # QoS 1, correlation required
  result:       picos/{source}/result/{subject}         # QoS 1, correlation required
  presence:     picos/{source}/presence                 # QoS 1, retained: true
Semantic messages in Steps 2–6 do not change. Swapping the transport means swapping this mapping file only. For a deeper walk-through of the adapter boundary — including a mock contract check that runs on local YAML — see the optional, non-runnable follow-up page: EMQX/MQTT as a transport adapter.

title: Lab · Give a Pico a Nervous System
text:
Step 11 — Reflect
Answer, using your files:

Which file expresses what capabilities the Pico offers (discovery)?
Which file expresses whether the Pico is reachable right now (presence)?
Why do the command, delegation, and result files name a capability or mission, and not an MQTT topic?
Why must the correlation on the result match the one on the delegation?
Which file expresses broker-side authentication and which expresses Open Engineering authorization, and why must they stay separate?
Which message becomes long-term memory, and why does an observation typically not?

title: 6. Nervous System
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

Explain why a Pico needs an event-driven communication fabric distinct from its Hands.
Distinguish Hands (act on external systems) from a Nervous System (sense, communicate, coordinate across distributed participants).
Describe a provider-neutral Pico Agent Transport and the semantic message types it carries.
Separate discovery, presence, delegation, result, and memory concerns.
Explain why identity and authorization MUST remain independent of the underlying transport, including MQTT client IDs.
Recognise EMQX/MQTT as a candidate implementation/adapter of the transport rather than the semantic owner or a credentialed prerequisite.

title: 6. Nervous System
section: A Pico that senses and coordinates
text:
A Pico that senses and coordinates
A Pico with Hands can change the world. To sense what is happening in the world, to communicate with other participants, and to coordinate work across distributed systems, it also needs an event-driven communication fabric. We call this capability a Nervous System.

A Pico without a Nervous System reasons and acts in isolation. A Pico with a Nervous System senses, communicates, and coordinates.

The resulting principle:

Open Engineering owns the semantics of what a Pico observes, publishes, commands, delegates, and discovers. Infrastructure providers implement the transport that carries those semantics.

title: 6. Nervous System
text:
Completing the Pico progression
The Part 3 lessons progressively equipped the learner’s Pico. This lesson adds the final faculty in the Part 3 progression:
Pico
│
├── Identity        →  Who am I?                    (lesson 01 · Pico Identity)
│
├── Senses          →  What is happening?           (lesson 02 · Cross-Mesh Communication, inbound)
│
├── Mind            →  What should I do?            (lesson 03 · Trust and Authorization + rules)
│
├── Voice           →  What should I communicate?   (lesson 02 · Cross-Mesh Communication, outbound)
│
├── Hands           →  What should I change         (lesson 05 · Hands)
│                      or execute?
│
└── Nervous System  →  How do I sense, discover,    (this lesson · 06 · Nervous System)
                       delegate, and coordinate
                       across many participants?
Hands and the Nervous System are not synonyms:

Hands decide how do I change this external system? — one action, one provider, one target.
A Nervous System decides how do I stay in touch with everything else? — many participants, event-driven, many-to-many.

Voice and Nervous System are also not synonyms. Voice is what a single Pico chooses to communicate. The Nervous System is the fabric across which many Voices, sensors, devices, and Picos exchange information.

title: 6. Nervous System
text:
Provider independence
Picos MUST NOT be architecturally dependent upon any particular broker or protocol. Open Engineering defines the abstract capability — the Pico Agent Transport — and any concrete transport becomes one implementation of that capability:
Pico
 │
 ▼
Pico Agent Transport
 │
 ├── MQTT / EMQX          (event-driven broker; this lesson's candidate)
 ├── A2A                  (agent-to-agent protocols)
 ├── in-process bus       (single-runtime tests, local development)
 └── future transports    (not yet chosen)
This follows the Open Engineering principle of separating Definition from Implementation. It is the same posture the Hands lesson takes with providers: rules and message semantics name transport-neutral concepts, and any concrete transport is an adapter behind that boundary.






ImportantEMQX/MQTT is a candidate adapter, not a credentialed prerequisite



This lesson treats EMQX and MQTT as one candidate implementation of the Pico Agent Transport. No exercise, lab step, or verification command in this wave provisions a live broker, opens an MQTT connection, or requires an EMQX account, TLS certificate, username, password, or API token. Every runnable check operates on local YAML using the provider-neutral message vocabulary. A separate, optional follow-up page — EMQX/MQTT as a transport adapter — shows the adapter mapping without running it.

title: 6. Nervous System
text:
The semantic message model
A Pico Agent Transport carries semantic messages, not raw bytes on a topic. The lesson distinguishes at least these message types, all provider-neutral and all named the same way regardless of the underlying transport:








Type
Meaning
Owned by




observation
Something is observed — sensor state, telemetry, a snapshot of reality.
sensing Pico or device


event
Something happened — a state transition that other participants may react to.
source Pico or system


command
A request to perform an action directed at a specific target.
requesting Pico


delegation
A Pico asks another Pico to carry out a mission.
delegating Pico


result
The outcome of a command, delegation, or mission.
executing Pico


presence
A Pico is available on the transport right now.
the Pico itself



Collapsing any two — for example, treating every command as an event or every observation as long-term memory — weakens the architecture. The exercise, lab, and quiz reinforce that they stay separate.
Every message carries at minimum:
envelope
├── type         (observation | event | command | delegation | result | presence)
├── source       (Pico identity of the sender)
├── target       (Pico identity or capability, for commands/delegations)
├── subject      (what the message is about — capability, resource, mission)
├── correlation  (request/response correlation ID)
├── timestamp    (when it was produced)
└── payload      (type-specific data)

text:
Authorization boundary
Authentication and authorization MUST remain separate. Being allowed to publish to a topic is not the same as being permitted to invoke the capability that topic represents. Broker authentication may answer “is this client permitted to open this connection?” Open Engineering must answer “is this Pico permitted to observe, command, or delegate this?”
Open Engineering                             Transport (e.g. MQTT / EMQX)
(identity · rules · policy ·                 (broker authentication ·
 capability authorization ·                   client IDs · topic ACLs ·
 delegation authorization ·                   sessions · QoS · retained
 evidence)                                    messages)
        │                                              │
        │  message: {type, source, target, subject}   │
        └───────────────► Transport Adapter ─────────►│
                          (topic naming,               │
                           delivery, retention)        ▼
                                                 Other participants

title: 6. Nervous System
section: Memory is not a side-effect of delivery
text:
Memory is not a side-effect of delivery
Events received through the Nervous System MUST NOT automatically become long-term memory. The Pico decides how to classify each incoming message:
Nervous System delivers a message
             │
             ▼
           Pico
             │
   ┌─────────┼─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
   ▼         ▼         ▼         ▼         ▼
 discard   observe   store     delegate    act
           (transient) (memory)  (mission)  (Hands)
Delivery is a communication concern. Classification and retention are cognitive concerns owned by Pico rules and memory, exactly as in the Trust and Authorization and Hands lessons.

Aspect
Hands
Nervous System




Purpose
Change an external system
Sense, communicate, coordinate

One capability, one target, one action
Many participants, many messages


Direction
Outbound action + evidence
Bidirectional and many-to-many


First runtime path

in-process bus · MQTT/EMQX · A2A · future

title: Quiz · Hands
text:
1. What distinguishes Mind from Hands?






TipShow answer





The Mind determines should I do this?; the Hands determine how do I do this?.

title: Quiz · Hands
text:
2. Why are Hands provider-neutral (capability-based)?






TipShow answer





So the Pico depends on capabilities like email.send rather than a provider’s tool names like GMAIL_SEND_EMAIL. The provider can then be swapped without changing Pico behaviour or rules.

title: Quiz · Hands
section: 3. What is the fundamental security rule for Hands?
text:
3. What is the fundamental security rule for Hands?






TipShow answer





No Hand acts without identity and authorization context. A valid credential does not imply authorization.

title: Quiz · Hands
section: 4. How are Hands different from MCP?
text:
4. How are Hands different from MCP?






TipShow answer





Hands are the Pico capability abstraction; MCP is an integration mechanism through which tools may be discovered or executed; Composio is a provider/platform. These concerns remain separate.

title: Quiz · Hands
section: 5. Name the seven concerns of a Hand invocation and who owns each.
text:
5. Name the seven concerns of a Hand invocation and who owns each.






TipShow answer






Composer equipment — Composer.
Pico decision — the Pico Mind.
Policy authorization — Open Engineering rules.
Hand selection — the Pico runtime.
Provider execution — the provider (local, Kubernetes, Composio, …).
Evidence — Pico memory.
Action event — the Pico Voice.

title: Quiz · Hands
section: 6. Why are evidence and the action event kept as separate artefacts?
text:
6. Why are evidence and the action event kept as separate artefacts?






TipShow answer





Evidence is a retainable, verifiable record of what actually happened, stored by the Pico so it can be audited or reasoned about later. The action event is a broadcast on the Pico’s Voice so other participants can subscribe and react. One serves memory and accountability; the other serves distributed communication. Collapsing them removes either auditability or reach.

title: Lab · Give a Pico Hands
text:
See the Open Engineering Language Server (OELS) onboarding guide for the local install and editor setup.
In this lab you will author one artefact per stage of a Hand invocation — Composer equipment, Pico decision, Policy authorization, Hand selection, Provider execution, Evidence, and Action event — and validate the local YAML with the pico CLI.
The scenario follows the memo progression: a Pico observes a condition, evaluates a rule, decides on an action, its Hand carries the action out, an evidence record is kept, and an action event is published.

title: Lab · Give a Pico Hands
text:
Setup
mkdir -p scratch/hands

title: Lab · Give a Pico Hands
section: Step 1 — Composer equipment (Pico definition with Hands)
text:
Step 1 — Composer equipment (Pico definition with Hands)
Create scratch/hands/pico.yaml. This is what the Composer puts on the Pico. It says only what capabilities are available, not what is permitted.
# scratch/hands/pico.yaml
apiVersion: open-engineering.io/v1alpha1
kind: Pico
metadata:
  name: issue-reporter
spec:
  hands:
    - name: external
      provider: local          # provider-neutral placeholder
      capabilities:
        - github.issue.read
        - github.issue.create
    - name: cluster
      provider: local          # provider-neutral placeholder
      capabilities:
        - kubernetes.resource.read

title: Lab · Give a Pico Hands
text:
Step 2 — Pico decision (governed action request)
Create scratch/hands/action.yaml — the “identity before action” boundary. This is the Pico’s decision to invoke a capability, not yet the authorization or the execution.
# scratch/hands/action.yaml
actor:
  pico: issue-reporter
principal:
  type: user
  id: user.example
action:
  capability: github.issue.create   # provider-neutral
authorization:
  capability: github.issue.create

title: Lab · Give a Pico Hands
text:
Step 3 — Policy authorization (rules with constraints)
Create scratch/hands/rules.yaml. These are the Open Engineering rules that decide whether the Pico’s decision is permitted in this context.
# scratch/hands/rules.yaml
rules:
  - capability: github.issue.create
    effect: allow
    constraints:
      repositories:
        - academy-test/*
  - capability: kubernetes.resource.read
    effect: allow
  - capability: kubernetes.resource.delete
    effect: deny
  - capability: github.issue.create
    effect: deny
    constraints:
      repositories:
        - production/*

title: Lab · Give a Pico Hands
text:
Step 4 — Hand selection
Create scratch/hands/selection.yaml. This records which specific Hand on the Pico is bound to carry out the authorized capability.
# scratch/hands/selection.yaml
selection:

title: 5. Hands
section: A Pico that can change the world
text:
A Pico that can change the world
A Pico can reason, observe, remember, communicate, and make decisions. To affect systems outside itself, however, it also needs a controlled mechanism for taking action. We call this capability Hands.

A Pico without Hands can understand the world. A Pico with Hands can change it.

The resulting principle:

A Composer equips a Pico with Hands. The Pico decides when to use them. A Hand performs the action. Open Engineering governs the whole loop.

title: 5. Hands
text:
Extending the Pico across Part 3
The previous Part 3 lessons progressively equipped the learner’s Pico. This lesson adds the final faculty in that progression:
Pico
│
├── Identity   →  Who am I?                (lesson 01 · Pico Identity)
│
├── Senses     →  What is happening?       (lesson 02 · Cross-Mesh Communication, inbound)
│
├── Mind       →  What should I do?        (lesson 03 · Trust and Authorization + rules)
│
├── Voice      →  What should I communicate? (lesson 02 · Cross-Mesh Communication, outbound)
│
└── Hands      →  What should I change     (this lesson · 05 · Hands)
                  or execute?
The distinction between Mind and Hands is particularly important:

The Mind determines: Should I do this?
The Hands determine: How do I do this?

Identity, Senses, Voice, and Mind were established earlier in Part 3. Hands build on all four — a Hand cannot act without identity, cannot know what to do without the Mind, cannot receive the trigger without Senses, and cannot report the outcome without Voice.

title: 5. Hands
text:
Provider independence
Picos MUST NOT be architecturally dependent upon any particular tool provider. Open Engineering defines the abstract capability — Pico Hands — and any concrete provider becomes one implementation of that capability:
Pico
 │
 ▼
Hands
 │
 ├── LocalHands       (in-process functions)
 ├── KubernetesHands  (cluster APIs)
 ├── PhysicalHands    (actuators, devices)
 └── ComposioHands    (external SaaS via Composio — optional)
This follows the Open Engineering principle of separating Definition from Implementation.






ImportantComposio and external providers — optional, non-runnable in this wave



This lesson treats Composio (and any other external SaaS provider) as illustrative only. No exercise, lab step, or verification command in this wave calls out to Composio, GitHub, Gmail, or Slack. The learner does not need any external accounts, tokens, or credentials to complete the lesson. All runnable checks operate on local YAML using the provider-neutral capability vocabulary.

title: 5. Hands
text:
The capability model
Hands should expose capabilities, not merely provider-specific tool names. For example:
github.issue.create
email.send
messaging.post
kubernetes.resource.read
mqtt.publish
servo.position.set
A provider maps these capabilities onto implementation-specific operations. For instance, email.send might map onto a hypothetical Composio tool such as GMAIL_SEND_EMAIL — but the Pico rule still names only email.send. This keeps Pico rules independent from any provider’s API vocabulary and lets the provider be swapped without changing the rules.

title: 5. Hands
text:
Identity before action
Hands MUST integrate with Pico identity. The fundamental security rule:

No Hand acts without identity and authorization context.

The Pico is not merely saying “send this email.” It is saying:
I am Pico X.
I am acting within this identity context.
My rules permit this capability.
My Hands provider can perform it.
Execute the requested action.

title: 5. Hands
text:
Authorization boundary
Authentication and authorization MUST remain conceptually separate. A valid credential MUST NOT imply authorization. Composio may answer “can this connected account authenticate to Gmail?” Open Engineering must answer “is this Pico permitted to send this email?”
Open Engineering
      │
      ├── Identity
      ├── Rules
      ├── Policy
      ├── Capability authorization
      └── Evidence
             │
             ▼
          Hands
             │
             ▼
          Composio
             │
             ▼
       External System

title: 5. Hands
text:
Governed execution
Hands integrate with Pico rules. Rules declare which capabilities are allowed, and richer rules constrain destinations, namespaces, environments, time windows, and approvals. For example:
capability: kubernetes.resource.apply
constraints:
  namespaces:
    - pico-*
  environments:
    - development
    - test
This turns Hands into governed execution rather than unrestricted tool calling. Some operations support human approval gates, so the architecture supports future human-in-the-loop execution.

title: 5. Hands
section: The seven concerns of a Hand invocation
text:
The seven concerns of a Hand invocation
A single Hand invocation crosses seven distinct concerns. The lesson lab produces one artefact for each of them.
1. Composer equipment
       │  what Hands the Pico is equipped with
       ▼
2. Pico decision
       │  the Mind chooses a capability to invoke
       ▼
3. Policy authorization
       │  Open Engineering rules say "yes, in this context"
       ▼
4. Hand selection
       │  the specific Hand (provider binding) is chosen
       ▼
5. Provider execution
       │  the underlying provider actually performs the action
       ▼
6. Evidence
       │  a signed record of what happened is kept
       ▼
7. Action event
          the Pico publishes a state-transition event via its Voice
Each concern belongs to a different actor:








Stage
Owned by
Answers




1 · Composer equipment
Composer
What Hands does this Pico even have?


2 · Pico decision
Pico Mind
Do I want to do this now?


3 · Policy authorization
Open Engineering rules
Am I allowed to do this here?


4 · Hand selection
Pico runtime
Which Hand should carry it out?


5 · Provider execution
Provider (Composio, k8s, local, …)
How does the outside world change?


6 · Evidence
Pico memory
What actually happened, verifiably?


7 · Action event
Pico Voice
Who else needs to know?



Collapsing any two of these — for example, equating provider authentication with policy authorization, or treating an action as its own evidence — weakens the architecture. The exercise, lab, and quiz reinforce that they stay separate.

title: 5. Hands
text:
Hands versus MCP
Hands and MCP should not be treated as synonyms. MCP may be one mechanism through which tools become discoverable or executable.
Pico
 ↓
Hands
 ↓
Provider / Protocol
 ├── Composio
 ├── MCP
 ├── REST
 ├── Kubernetes
 ├── MQTT
 └── local execution
Hands are the Pico capability abstraction. MCP is an integration mechanism. Composio is a provider/platform. These concerns remain separate.

title: 3. Trust and Authorization

Identity does not replace authorization
A particularly useful design decision is that the new DID infrastructure does not replace the existing Pico channel authorization model. The responsibilities remain separate.
DID

 └── Who is the other party?
Channel / ECI policy
 │

A subscription’s peer DID acts as its channel identity, while existing channel policy determines what that relationship may do.
This gives Open Engineering an important architectural principle:

Identity establishes who; policy establishes what.

The Pico Engine therefore gains cryptographic identity without requiring its authorization model to be rewritten at the same time.

title: Summary · Cross-Mesh Communication
text:
A subscription is a pairwise relationship represented on both sides. One side initiates using the recipient’s did:webvh; the handshake resolves the identity and creates peer DIDs.
Once established, events and queries use the did:peer relationship — not the public did:webvh.
DIDComm provides encrypted cross-mesh and cross-engine communication using the peer relationship. Within the same mesh, traffic can stay local.
Two relationship classes exist: family (parent/child, ECI-based, no DID needed) and external (subscriptions, did:webvh → introduction, did:peer → established relationship).
DID-based introduction would be unnecessary overhead for relationships already established structurally within a Pico family.

Isolation. If one relationship is compromised, its peer DID can be rotated, removed, or recreated without changing the Pico’s other relationships, and no single relationship can reveal the others.

title: 1. Pico Identity
text:
Identity, not just address
Before Pico Engine 1.6, a channel identifier could answer one question:

How do I communicate with this Pico on this engine?

It could not answer a more durable one:

Which Pico is this?

Version 1.6 gives every Pico its own cryptographic identity. That identity is intended to travel with the Pico rather than merely identify where it currently happens to execute.






Tip



Think of a channel (an ECI) as a mailbox and a DID as the person who owns the mailbox. Mailboxes move and change; the person is who they are.

title: 1. Pico Identity
text:
Two DIDs, two responsibilities
Every Pico uses two kinds of Decentralized Identifiers:
Pico
│
├── did:webvh
│   └── Public / portable Pico identity
│
└── did:peer
    ├── Relationship A
    ├── Relationship B
    └── Relationship C
The distinction is deliberate. A Pico should not expose one universal identifier for every relationship it participates in. The architecture separates identity from relationship identity.

title: 1. Pico Identity
1. Pico Identity
text:
did:peer — the relationship identity
Once two Picos decide to establish a relationship, they create pairwise did:peer identities. A new pair is created for each relationship.
Pico A          Pico B
did:webvh:A     did:webvh:B
      │
      └── introduction ──▶ subscription
                              │
                          A → did:peer:A-B
                          B → did:peer:B-A
These peer DIDs are private to that relationship. A useful analogy:
did:webvh = passport
did:peer  = private address given to one relationship
This provides significant isolation. If a relationship is compromised, its peer DID can be rotated, removed, or recreated without changing the Pico’s other relationships.
Pico
 ├── Relationship A → did:peer:...
 ├── Relationship B → did:peer:...
 └── Relationship C → did:peer:...
Relationship B can be replaced without affecting A or C.

title: 1. Pico Identity
text:
Why not one universal DID?
A single identifier used everywhere would let any party correlate every relationship a Pico participates in. Pairwise did:peer identities keep relationships separate so that no single relationship can reveal the others.
This is the same isolation principle you will see again in Trust and Authorization.

section: 1. In one sentence, what is capability composition / resolution, and how is it different from rule compilation?
text:
1. In one sentence, what is capability composition / resolution, and how is it different from rule compilation?






TipShow answer





Capability composition / resolution takes one Pico definition and a set of installed capsule definitions and produces a resolved composition manifest that pins each spec.capabilities entry to a specific capsule (memo2 §4 D4). Rule compilation is what bin/pico compose does in this repository: it turns one parsed Rule into one executable shell-script artefact and currently handles only kind: greeting (verified in memo24.md §2.4). The two operations live in different repositories; the Academy ships neither resolver nor a new validator (memo2 §4 D4 Consequences for the Academy). See the lesson.

title: Quiz · Compose a Pico
section: 2. Classify foo.bar@0.1.0, foo.bar@1.2.0, foo.bar@=1.0.0, and foo.bar.
text:
2. Classify foo.bar@0.1.0, foo.bar@1.2.0, foo.bar@=1.0.0, and foo.bar.






TipShow answer





From memo2 §2 D2:

foo.bar@0.1.0 — caret (0.x variant). Resolves against any foo.bar capsule whose version has the same minor 1 and patch ≥ 0.
foo.bar@1.2.0 — caret on the ≥ 1.0 line. Same major (1) and version ≥ 1.2.0.
foo.bar@=1.0.0 — exact. Strict equality on metadata.version.
foo.bar — bare. Matches any version of a foo.bar provider.

title: Quiz · Compose a Pico
section: 3. The lab’s capsule provides oe.greeting at 0.1.0. Why does oe.greeting@=0.2.0 fail where oe.greeting@0.1.0 succeeds?
text:
3. The lab’s capsule provides oe.greeting at 0.1.0. Why does oe.greeting@=0.2.0 fail where oe.greeting@0.1.0 succeeds?






TipShow answer





@=0.2.0 is an exact-match constraint; it requires metadata.version == 0.2.0. The installed capsule is at 0.1.0, so zero candidates survive the version check and the resolver returns outcome: error, error: no-matching-provider, requirement: oe.greeting@=0.2.0. @0.1.0 is a caret constraint on a 0.x line; it requires the same minor and patch ≥ 0, which 0.1.0 satisfies exactly — so the same capsule succeeds. See the exercise Task B and upstream fixture fixtures/scenarios/exact-nomatch-patch.yaml.

title: Quiz · Compose a Pico
section: 4. Two installed capsules both provide foo.bar and both satisfy a Pico’s bare foo.bar requirement. What does a conforming resolver emit at v0.1, and why can you not just pick one in spec.composition?
text:
4. Two installed capsules both provide foo.bar and both satisfy a Pico’s bare foo.bar requirement. What does a conforming resolver emit at v0.1, and why can you not just pick one in spec.composition?






TipShow answer





It emits outcome: error, error: multiple-matching-providers, requirement: foo.bar, and lists both candidate providers (upstream fixture fixtures/scenarios/duplicate-provider.yaml). In v0.1, more than one matching provider is an explicit error — memo2 §3 D3 §2 amendment: “resolving to more than one matching provider is an explicit error (memo23 §5 rule 9 ‘Graceful failure’)”. The spec.composition block that would let a Pico pick one is reserved for v0.2 and is upstream-owned; v0.1 Picos SHOULD NOT declare it, and the Academy will not add such a block locally.

title: Quiz · Compose a Pico
section: 5. A requirement reads foo.bar@0.1.0 and the installed capsule is foo.bar at 0.2.0. Does 0.x caret cross a minor boundary?
text:
5. A requirement reads foo.bar@0.1.0 and the installed capsule is foo.bar at 0.2.0. Does 0.x caret cross a minor boundary?






TipShow answer





No. memo2 §2 D2 states explicitly that for 0.x versions caret requires the same minor and patch ≥ requested; a different minor is a non-match. The resolver emits outcome: error, error: no-matching-provider, requirement: foo.bar@0.1.0 (upstream fixture fixtures/scenarios/zerox-different-minor-nomatch.yaml). Contrast this with the ≥ 1.0 line, where caret crosses minor and patch within the same major (fixtures/scenarios/caret-match.yaml).

No change is needed. definitions/pico.yaml already requires spec.capabilities: [string]; each item is a capability identifier (optionally plus a constraint) per memo2 §3 D3 §2 amendment. No new required field is added and the Academy does not introduce spec.composition locally. title: Quiz · Compose a Pico
section: 7. Which capability identifiers below are grammar-conformant, and which are not? Give the memo2 §3 D3 reason for each rejection.
text:
7. Which capability identifiers below are grammar-conformant, and which are not? Give the memo2 §3 D3 reason for each rejection.
oe.greeting, pico.state.set, Greeting, oe..greeting, oe_greeting, github.issue.create






TipShow answer





Conformant: oe.greeting, pico.state.set, github.issue.create — each is two or more dot-separated segments, every segment starts with a lower-case ASCII letter, and only [a-z0-9] or single internal hyphens appear.
Non-conformant:

Greeting — upper-case leading letter and single segment (needs at least one .).
oe..greeting — empty segment between the two dots.
oe_greeting — underscore is not in the segment alphabet; also no dot separator.

See upstream fixtures invalid/capability-upper-case.yaml, invalid/capability-empty-segment.yaml, and invalid/capability-underscore.yaml.

Prerequisites

title: 4. Compose a Pico
text:
Two terms, kept separate
Upstream memo2 §4 D4 fixes this terminology for the Academy and the Pico ecosystem. Keep the two apart; they refer to different operations in different repositories.

Rule compilation — what bin/pico compose in this repository does. Input: one parsed Rule (today only kind: greeting). Output: one executable shell-script artefact. Verified in memo24.md §2.4. It does not read capsule definitions, it does not resolve spec.capabilities, and it does not check version compatibility.
Capability composition / resolution — the new operation defined in memo2 §4 D4. Input: one Pico definition and a set of installed capsule definitions. Output: a resolved composition manifest that pins each entry of spec.capabilities to a specific capsule metadata.name + version. The normative semantics live in open-engineering-capsules/source; the reference command-line implementation lives in open-engineering-capsule/source (memo2 §1 D1, §4 D4). The Academy ships no resolver and will not fork validation (memo2 §4 D4 Consequences for the Academy).

title: 4. Compose a Pico
text:
The capability-identifier binding (memo2 §3 D3)
A Pico says what capability it needs in its existing spec.capabilities: [string] field (the Academy’s definitions/pico.yaml requires this field; no schema change here, see Lesson 1 — Understand a Pico). Each item is a capability identifier — matching the grammar below — optionally followed by a version constraint.
A capsule says what capability it provides through its spec.capability field, whose value is a single capability identifier matching the same grammar.
Resolution walks every item of spec.capabilities and keeps the installed capsules whose spec.capability equals the identifier and whose metadata.version satisfies the stated constraint. The outcomes are fixed:

Exactly one surviving provider → outcome: resolved.
Zero surviving providers → outcome: error, error: no-matching-provider.
Two or more surviving providers → outcome: error, error: multiple-matching-providers. In v0.1, explicit provider selection is not available; spec.composition is reserved for v0.2 (memo2 §3 D3 §2 amendment).


Grammar (memo2 §3 D3)
Capability identifiers are two or more dot-separated lower-case segments:
^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*(\.[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*)+$
Accepted: oe.greeting, github.issue.create, pico.state.set. Rejected: Greeting (upper-case, single segment), oe..greeting (empty segment), oe_greeting (underscore, no dot separator).


Version constraints (memo2 §2 D2)








Form
Constraint
Match rule




name (bare)
any
Any metadata.version matches.


name@X.Y.Z (X ≥ 1)
caret
Same major as X, version ≥ X.Y.Z.


name@0.Y.Z
caret (0.x)
Same minor Y, patch ≥ Z.


name@=X.Y.Z
exact
metadata.version strictly equals X.Y.Z.



Every metadata.version MUST itself be a valid SemVer 2.0.0 string.

title: 4. Compose a Pico
text:
Worked resolution — the oe.greeting example
Upstream memo1 §3 publishes the following Pico and capsule side by side. Here we resolve the Pico against the capsule by hand, using the memo2 rules.
Pico (requires one capability):
apiVersion: open-engineering.io/v1alpha1
kind: Pico
metadata:
  name: hello-pico
spec:
  type: greeter
  capabilities:
    - oe.greeting@0.1.0
  implementation: {}
  state: {}
  events: {}
Capsule (installed; provides one capability):
apiVersion: open-engineering.io/v1alpha1
kind: Capsule
metadata:
  name: greeting
  version: 0.1.0
spec:
  capability: oe.greeting
  inputs:
    value: { type: string, required: true }
  outputs:
    greeting: { type: string }
  dependencies: []
Steps:

Parse the requirement. oe.greeting@0.1.0 → identifier oe.greeting, version suffix @0.1.0. Per memo2 §2 D2 the leading @ without = is a caret constraint.
Grammar check (§3 D3). oe.greeting matches the pattern — two segments, both start with a lower-case letter, no illegal character. The capsule’s spec.capability is identical. ✔
Enumerate candidate providers. Among installed capsules, those whose spec.capability equals oe.greeting: one match — greeting at version 0.1.0.
Apply the version constraint (§2 D2, 0.x rule). For 0.x, caret requires the same minor and patch ≥ Z. Requirement 0.1.0 → candidate 0.1.0: same minor (1), patch 0 ≥ 0. ✔
Check uniqueness (§3 D3 §2 amendment). Exactly one candidate survives; two or more would be error: multiple-matching-providers. ✔
Emit the resolution.

outcome: resolved
resolution:
  - requirement: oe.greeting@0.1.0
    constraint: caret
    provider: { name: greeting, version: "0.1.0" }
That block is byte-equivalent to the expected block of the upstream fixtures/scenarios/resolve-greeting.yaml fixture at pinned commit bf071c2c1b57 — the worked fixture under memo2 §5 follow-up (a).

title: Summary · Implement and test a capsule
text:
A capsule’s spec.inputs and spec.outputs are the only public surface an implementation may rely on. Everything else — language, state, internal libraries — is implementation detail that the contract neither sees nor constrains.
A capsule implementation keeps its third-party dependencies local to itself. The reference oe.greeting implementation needs none; Python stdlib suffices. If a capability needed httpx, it would be pinned in that capsule implementation’s own manifest, not in bin/pico and not in a sibling capsule.
Unit tests cover specific behaviour (e.g. greeting({"value": "Pico"}) returns {"greeting": "Hello, Pico!"}). Contract tests are derived at test time from capsule.yaml and catch drift between code and contract (e.g. a renamed output key, a changed declared type, a new required input the implementation does not handle). The split keeps one source of truth for the contract and one for the implementation.
A declared-required input that is absent raises a named, catchable exception (MissingRequiredInput("value")) that carries the input’s name — not a generic KeyError and not a stack trace. Satisfies memo23 §5 rule 9 (Graceful failure) at the capability boundary.
Diagnostics belong on logging, not a framework: log the capability identifier and metadata.version once per process at the first call, and log each MissingRequiredInput with the input name. The reference stdlib implementation ships without the log calls today; the exercise walks through where they would go.
The call shape used in this lesson (greeting(inputs: dict) -> dict) is a course-local teaching harness. The implementation convention for capsules belongs to open-engineering-capsule/source (memo2 §1 D1), which has published none yet (memo24.md §2.1 as updated by observation at upstream commit bf071c2c1b57). When published, the Academy will consume it (memo23.md §3.2, memo26.md §5).

A declared-required input that is absent raises a named, catchable exception (MissingRequiredInput("value")) that carries the input’s name — not a generic KeyError and not a stack trace. Satisfies memo23 §5 rule 9 (Graceful failure) at the capability boundary.
Diagnostics belong on logging, not a framework: log the capability identifier and metadata.version once per process at the first call, and log each MissingRequiredInput with the input name. The reference stdlib implementation ships without the log calls today; the exercise walks through where they would go.
The call shape used in this lesson (greeting(inputs: dict) -> dict) is a course-local teaching harness. The implementation convention for capsules belongs to open-engineering-capsule/source (memo2 §1 D1), which has published none yet (memo24.md §2.1 as updated by observation at upstream commit bf071c2c1b57). When published, the Academy will consume it (memo23.md §3.2, memo26.md §5).

Minimal core. The Pico core does not import greeting.py; a future Composer would resolve a capability requirement to any capsule whose spec.capability matches.

Graceful failure. MissingRequiredInput names the missing input; no generic exceptions escape the capability boundary.
Observable operation. Capability identifier and version are logged at first call; each structured error is logged with its input name (framework-free logging).

text:
What a capsule is
A capsule is a declarative contract for one capability. The adopted v0.1 contract is a kind: Capsule document with four groups of required fields and a small set of optional fields. The normative schema lives at capsule.schema.json in open-engineering-capsules/source at commit bf071c2c1b57; the accompanying conformance fixture set is the executable arbiter of what a conforming capsule looks like.

title: 1. Define a capsule
section: Required and optional fields at v0.1
text:
Required and optional fields at v0.1
The table below is reproduced from memo1 §1 at bf071c2c1b57. Required fields are the smallest set the course Modules 2–4 cannot be taught without; every other field listed in memo23 §3.2 is optional at v0.1 with a stated rationale.








Required field
Role
Why required at v0.1




apiVersion, kind, metadata.name, metadata.version
Identity and version
Module 2 cannot address a capsule or pin a version without them.


spec.capability
Capability name
Module 4 must bind a Pico’s declared capability requirement to exactly one capsule by name.


spec.inputs, spec.outputs
Inputs and outputs
Module 3 tests a capsule against its contract; a contract with no inputs/outputs is not testable.


spec.dependencies
Capability dependencies
Module 4’s dependency resolution and memo23 §5 rule 3 (Explicit dependencies) require declared dependencies; may be [].



Optional at v0.1 (each with a one-line rationale in memo1 §1): spec.purpose, spec.interfaces, spec.events, spec.config, spec.secrets, spec.lifecycle, spec.compatibility, spec.health, spec.tests, spec.permissions, spec.resources. v0.1 picks the smallest field set that keeps Modules 2–4 teachable; the owning repository may promote any optional field to required in a later version.

A valid minimal capsule
The worked example from memo1 §3, restated at the identifier grammar adopted in memo2 §3 D3 and published verbatim as fixtures/valid/greeting.yaml:
apiVersion: open-engineering.io/v1alpha1
kind: Capsule
metadata:
  name: greeting
  version: 0.1.0
spec:
  capability: oe.greeting
  inputs:
    value:
      type: string
      required: true
  outputs:
    greeting:
      type: string
  dependencies: []

title: 1. Define a capsule
text:
Capability identifier grammar (memo2 §3 D3)
A capability identifier is two or more dot-separated lower-case segments; each segment starts with a lower-case ASCII letter and otherwise contains lower-case ASCII letters, ASCII digits, or single internal hyphens. The pattern, published in memo2 §3 D3 and enforced by capsule.schema.json:
^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*(\.[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*)+$
Conforming examples (every conforming validator MUST accept): oe.greeting, github.issue.create, pico.state.set.
Non-conforming examples (every conforming validator MUST reject): Greeting (single segment, upper-case start), oe..greeting (empty segment), oe_greeting (underscore not in the segment alphabet).

text:
Version compatibility constraints (memo2 §2 D2)
Every metadata.version MUST be a valid SemVer 2.0.0 string. memo2 §2 D2 defines three constraint forms a Pico may write in its spec.capabilities:







Written form
Meaning




oe.greeting
Bare — any version matches.


oe.greeting@0.1.0
Caret — same major and version ≥ 0.1.0; for 0.x, same minor and patch ≥ 0.


oe.greeting@=0.1.0
Exact — only 0.1.0 matches.

title: 1. Define a capsule
text:
Contract, not implementation
A capsule document is a contract: it names a capability, declares inputs and outputs by name and type, and pins a version — nothing more. It carries no code and no runtime concern. The code that satisfies the contract is a capsule implementation, which belongs to open-engineering-capsule/source (the implementation org, memo2 §1 D1); the Academy does not fork or shadow it (memo23 §3.2). A Pico composes a capability by writing a capability identifier into its spec.capabilities; the reference validator resolves that identifier to any installed capsule whose spec.capability matches and whose metadata.version satisfies the stated constraint (memo2 §3 D3, fixtures/scenarios/resolve-greeting.yaml). The contract is what makes two independent implementations substitutable; everything specific to one implementation stays inside that implementation.

title: Quiz · Understand a Pico

text:
6. Why is coupling a Pico’s core directly to a database, broker, or AI library costly?






TipShow answer





Because every test, every environment, and every learner inherits the install, runtime, and version-skew burden of each dependency even when the capability under test does not need it. Keeping capabilities behind capsule contracts keeps implementation-specific dependencies local to the capability that uses them, so the core and every other capability remain testable in isolation. This is the motivation behind memo23 §5 rules 1–3 (minimal core, optional by default, explicit dependencies).

title: 1. Understand a Pico
section: What a Pico is (and is not)
text:
What a Pico is (and is not)
A Pico is a small declarative Open Engineering artifact. The Pico core is responsible for composition and the agreed runtime boundary; every other concern — persistence, messaging, AI inference, tool integration, bot interfaces, operations — belongs to a capability that the Pico composes only when it needs it.
A Pico should not require a framework stack to exist. If adding one capability forces the learner to install Kubernetes, a database, or a message broker, the capability has been baked into the core rather than composed into it.

Four terms, one sentence each

Capability — a named, provider-neutral action or function a Pico may need (for example greeting, email.send, or github.issue.create).
Capsule definition — a declarative contract describing one capability (identity, version, inputs, outputs, dependencies). This shape is proposed upstream and does not yet exist as a committed schema — see the callout below.
Capsule implementation — the concrete code that satisfies a capsule definition behind its contract, keeping third-party dependencies local to the implementation.
Composed Pico — a Pico built by selecting a minimal core and binding the capsule capabilities it needs, not by hard-wiring a framework stack into the core.

title: 1. Understand a Pico
text:
What definitions/pico.yaml requires today
definitions/pico.yaml is the OE Pico artefact contract this repository ships. Its target schema requires exactly these fields on an OE-shaped Pico:
apiVersion
kind
metadata.name
spec.type
spec.capabilities      (list of capability names; may be empty)
spec.implementation
spec.state
spec.events
The Pico anatomy listed in open-engineering-picos/source/memo7.md (verified in memo24.md §2.3) — Face (Python), Muscles (Rust+PyO3), Memory (Celld), Hands (Composio), Nervous System (EMQX), Rules (OE Rules), Discovery (A2A), Operations (Open Engineering Operations) — is not named by definitions/pico.yaml as a required field. The schema requires none of these anatomy items by name; each is a capability a Pico composes when its stated purpose needs it.






ImportantCapsules are not a committed upstream contract yet



Verification on 2026-10-16 (recorded in memo24.md §2.1) found that open-engineering-capsules/source contains only README.md and a generated-placeholder metadata.yaml (lifecycle: proposed). No capsule schema, convention, worked example, Composer, lifecycle document, or dependency model is committed upstream.
The capsule shape used in this lesson — kind: Capsule with spec.capability, spec.inputs, spec.outputs, spec.dependencies — is the memo26 proposal addressed to open-engineering-capsules/source. It is not yet adopted upstream and this course does not ask you to author or validate a capsule file. When the owning repository publishes a canonical contract, the course will consume whatever is published.

title: 1. Understand a Pico
section: Why coupling the core to frameworks is costly
text:
Why coupling the core to frameworks is costly
A Pico whose core depends directly on a particular database, broker, AI library, or bot platform inherits the install, runtime, and version-skew burden of each one. The consequences are concrete:

A test for the greeting logic cannot run without starting the broker, the database, and the bot runtime.
Replacing one dependency means editing the core instead of swapping one capsule implementation behind its contract.
Learners must install the full stack to run the simplest example, which is exactly what today’s labs/hello-pico avoids by requiring only a shell, a text editor, and Python 3.

The capsule-first mental model keeps implementation-specific dependencies inside the capability that needs them, so the core — and every other capability — stays testable in isolation.

title: 1. Understand a Pico
section: The current Rules → Parser → Composer → Pico pipeline
text:
The current Rules → Parser → Composer → Pico pipeline
The reference bin/pico CLI (bin/pico) implements the pipeline the labs already use:
Rules  ─────▶  Parser         ─────▶  Composer        ─────▶  Pico artefact
(YAML)         (pico parse)           (pico compose)          (hello-world-pico)
Composed-core view (ASCII, not to scale):
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
          │              Pico (core)                 │
          │  responsibilities: composition and the   │
          │  agreed runtime boundary — nothing more  │
          └───────┬─────────┬─────────┬──────────────┘
                  │         │         │
            ┌─────▼───┐ ┌───▼────┐ ┌──▼─────────┐
            │ capsule │ │ capsule│ │ capsule    │   ← each capsule declares
            │ (e.g.   │ │ (e.g.  │ │ (e.g.      │     a capability and keeps
            │ greet-  │ │ memory)│ │ transport) │     its dependencies local
            │ ing)    │ │        │ │            │
            └─────────┘ └────────┘ └────────────┘
Today the pipeline is dependency-free and runs end-to-end against only Python 3 and bin/pico. The exercise and lab stay inside that pipeline.






Note“Composer” today means pico compose, not capability composition



In this repository the Composer (defined in the Glossary) is a Rules → artefact code generator: pico compose reads a parsed Rule, requires kind: greeting, and writes an executable shell script that prints the Rule’s value (bin/pico lines 105–109, verified in memo24.md §2.4). It is not a capability composer: it does not resolve capsule dependencies, bind interfaces, or check compatibility across capsule contracts. Capability composition is a separate concept that would require an upstream decision (see memo26 §4 open question 4). The two senses of “compose” are kept apart in this course.

title: Formal realization schema
text:
The Hello Pico record
The reference instance data expresses, in formal form, the same path the course already teaches:
Definition -> Realization -> Element -> Validation

Definition — hello-pico-definition names three Constraints: exact output, Kubernetes Job form, and successful completion.
Realization — hello-pico-realization-v1 realizes the Definition and uses the Sandcastle, Crossplane, and MiniKube Dependencies.
Element — hello-pico-job-001 conforms to the Definition and carries the observed output Hello, Pico!.
Validations — three checks, one per Constraint, each recorded as passed.

title: Constructive realization
text:
This page is the course-facing reference for the academy’s small constructive-realization vocabulary. It is written for learners and course authors working in the Pico course; the underlying contract lives in templates/README.qmd (in-repo scaffold, not published as a learner page; Phase 1).
Phase 1 is documentation and metadata only. Nothing here changes how a Pico is built; it names the concepts you are already using so lessons, labs, and metadata can point at them consistently.

title: Constructive realization
text:
The five terms

Definition — what an artifact is supposed to be: its purpose, intent, and expected outcome. In this course, a Pico’s Rules together with the surrounding lesson framing state a Definition.
Element — the concrete realized thing. In this course, a running hello-world-pico produced by the pipeline is an Element.
Realization — the constructive path from Definition to Element. In this course, the Rules → Parser → Composer → Pico pipeline is the Realization, and the Hello Pico lab records it step by step.
Constraint — a condition a valid Element must satisfy (for example: “the Pico responds to the hello event”, “the Rules parse without error”).
Validation — an executable or observable check that tests an Element against its Constraints (for example: a lab’s verify.sh, a course quiz, or an end-to-end lab walkthrough).

title: Constructive realization
text:
Mapping onto the Pico pipeline
The pipeline you already know maps cleanly onto the vocabulary:
Rules  ─────▶  Parser  ─────▶  Composer  ─────▶  Pico
(Definition)   (Realization)   (Realization)     (Element)

Rules carry the Definition of the Pico you intend to build.
Parser + Composer are the Realization: the constructive path that turns a Definition into an Element.
Pico (for example hello-world-pico) is the Element.
Constraints are the conditions the produced Pico must meet.
Validations are the checks — lab verifications, quizzes, observable behavior — that confirm the Element satisfies its Constraints.

title: Constructive realization
text:
Mapping onto compose → construct → behave
The academy’s three-layer story — Crossplane composes, Sandcastle constructs, Picos behave — is a story about Realization at three different scales:







Layer
Constructive-realization view




Crossplane composes
Realization by composition from sub-elements; a composed resource is the Element.


Sandcastle constructs
The bounded engineering environment inside which Realizations safely run and produce Elements.


Picos behave
The Elements themselves at runtime; their behavior is the observable evidence of Realization.



Concretely, in this course:

The Pico course teaches how a single Pico Element behaves.
The Crossplane course teaches how such Elements are composed on a control plane.
The Sandcastle course teaches the construction environment inside which Realization happens safely.

title: Constructive realization
section: Where the terms show up in course material
text:
Where the terms show up in course material
You will most often encounter these concepts in the places you already work:

Course and lesson index.qmd — typically states a Definition (learning objectives, what the produced artifact is).
lab.qmd and the shared labs/ — typically records a Realization and the Element it produces.
metadata.yaml — the machine-readable side of the same story. The Phase 1 fields (constructive_role, realizes, constraints, validated_by, realization_pattern) are optional and additive; see templates/README.qmd (in-repo scaffold, not published as a learner page) for the full contract.
quiz.qmd and lab verifications — natural places for Validations that check an Element against its Constraints.

title: Constructive realization
text:
Authoring guidance for this course

Prefer natural-language Constraints in prose and named Validations (a verify.sh, a quiz question, an observable behavior) over formal schemas.
When a lesson produces a named artifact, treat that artifact name as the Element identity; a downstream lab realizes the same Definition when it lists it under realizes in its metadata.
Do not retrofit existing pico lessons or labs to the new metadata fields as part of this reference — the Phase 1 fields are optional and sit alongside existing metadata.

title: Constructive realization
text:
Hands as a governed extension
Part 3 introduces Hands — the controlled mechanism through which a Pico acts on the world. Hands slot into the same constructive vocabulary rather than sitting outside it, and they line up with the Phase 7 runtime/control-surface contract in templates/README.qmd (in-repo scaffold, not published as a learner page).
The mapping is:







Hands concept
Constructive-realization view




Capability (e.g. github.issue.create)
A Definition of an action the Pico is meant to be able to perform, stated in a Rule.


HandsProvider (ComposioHands, …)
A Realization step: the constructive path from a Capability Definition to an executed act.


ActionRequest + ExecutionContext
The Definition of one specific attempt to act, carrying identity, authorization, and Policy.


Hand execution on a HandsProvider
The Realization producing the acted-upon Element (an issue created, a resource applied).


Policy
A Constraint on the ActionRequest — the same Phase 1 Constraint concept, scoped to a Capability.


Evidence and Action Events
Validations and Observations: they record whether the executed action satisfied its Constraints.



Hands stay provider-neutral: Pico rules name Capabilities, not provider tool names, so the HandsProvider Realization step can be swapped (Composio, Kubernetes, local, MQTT, physical) without changing the Capability Definitions the Pico depends on. This mirrors the Phase 7 rule that ControlSurfaces and runtime environments must not replace or bypass the constructive chain.

title: Constructive realization
section: Nervous system as a governed extension
text:
Nervous system as a governed extension
The course also introduces a Nervous System — the provider-neutral communication fabric through which a Pico senses, communicates, coordinates, and interacts with other Picos, devices, and services. The Nervous System sits after Hands in the Pico progression and is distinct from Brain/Mind, Hands, and Voice: Brain/Mind decides whether to act, Hands decide how to act on external systems, Voice decides what to communicate outward, and the Nervous System is the transport-neutral fabric those messages travel through.
Like Hands, the Nervous System slots into the same constructive vocabulary rather than sitting outside it, and it lines up with the Phase 7 runtime/control-surface contract in templates/README.qmd (in-repo scaffold, not published as a learner page).
The mapping is:







Nervous System concept
Constructive-realization view




Pico Agent Transport
A Realization step: the constructive path from a Nervous System message Definition to a delivered message.


Message Envelope
The Definition of a single message: type, identity, correlation, timestamp, payload — stated independently of wire format.


Observation (course-scoped)
A runtime-captured Observation in the Phase 7 sense; a candidate input to Feedback that MAY refine a Definition.


Event
A named runtime occurrence carried through a Phase 7 Channel as a typed EventType value.


Command
The Definition of a requested action; the receiving Pico’s Rules provide its Realization, and Policy is its Constraint.


Delegation
The Definition of a mission handed to another Pico; the delegate’s Rules and Policy are its Realization and Constraints.


Result
A Validation of a Command or Delegation: the observable outcome recorded against the original request’s Constraints.


Presence
A runtime-captured Observation about a Pico’s transport availability; not a Capability claim.


Discovery
A Definition-facing lookup of what Capabilities are advertised; it does not by itself authorize invocation.


Topic Authorization
A Constraint on the transport pathway an envelope may traverse.


Capability Authorization
A Constraint on which Capabilities a specific Identity may invoke — the same Constraint concept Policy applies to Hands.



The Nervous System stays provider-neutral: Pico rules and Hands name Capabilities and Nervous System message types, not transport-specific identifiers, so the transport Realization step can be swapped (MQTT via EMQX, a future A2A binding, an in-process transport) without changing the Nervous System Definitions the Pico depends on. This mirrors the Phase 7 rule that ControlSurfaces and runtime environments must not replace or bypass the constructive chain, and the Hands rule that HandsProviders must not become the Pico’s semantic owner.
Identity, Authorization, Evidence, and Memory boundaries remain the same across Hands and the Nervous System:

Identity is required context on every envelope; the transport’s own client/session identifiers MUST NOT be treated as the Pico’s Identity.
Authorization is decided by Policy on the semantic layer; Topic Authorization at the transport is necessary but not sufficient, and a valid transport credential MUST NOT be treated as Capability Authorization.
Evidence records what a governed exchange did — the acting Pico, the requested Capability, the authorization decision, the lifecycle of the request — without carrying transport credentials or raw payloads.
Memory remains a Pico-side decision: an Observation or Event received through the Nervous System is not automatically Memory. The Pico’s Rules decide whether it becomes Evidence, a Memory candidate, or is discarded.

The existing Rules → Parser → Composer → Pico pipeline and the Part 3 · Hands contract remain unchanged; the Nervous System is an additive layer alongside them.

title: Constructive realization
section: Out of scope on this page
text:
Out of scope on this page
This page intentionally does not:

Introduce a formal ontology, schema, or conformance checker.
Change the Pico pipeline, lesson layout, or lab format.
Retrofit existing courses, lessons, or labs to the Phase 1 fields.
Add HandsProvider SDKs, credentials, or external integrations; those are out of scope for the course contract and belong to separate provider-follow-up work.
Add transport SDKs, broker credentials, or a specific MQTT/EMQX deployment; the Nervous System contract names transport-neutral semantics and leaves broker adapters, credentials, and schema-enforcement tooling to separate follow-up work.

See the Glossary for one-line definitions of these terms and the course overview for how the pieces fit together. For a fully worked example that points each term at concrete Hello Pico material, see Hello Pico as a constructive exemplar.

title: Pico
text: Welcome to Pico, the reference course of the Open Engineering Academy. This course teaches how to design and build your first Pico — a small, declarative, composable engineering artifact — and doubles as the canonical example for how every academy course website is structured.

title: Pico
text:
Where this course fits
Pico is the academy’s behaviour layer. The three-layer story is:

Crossplane composes, Sandcastle constructs, Picos behave.

This course teaches what a Pico does at runtime — how a hello-world-pico receives events, evaluates rules, and produces actions. Its sibling courses teach the other two layers:

Crossplane course — declares and composes what should exist on a control plane.
Sandcastle course — the bounded engineering environment inside which artifacts like Picos are safely built.

Pico is the foundation for the other two: complete this course first so you know what a durable Pico artifact looks like before you compose it with Crossplane or construct it inside a Sandcastle.

title: Pico
text:
What you will learn
By the end of the course you will be able to:

Explain what a Pico is and how it fits into Open Engineering.
Author Rules, a Parser, and a Composer for a minimal Pico.
Produce a working hello-world-pico and describe it with metadata.
Distinguish a Pico’s Mind (whether/why it should act) from its Hands (how an action is executed), and explain why Hands stay provider-neutral. See Part 3 · Hands.
Place a Pico’s Nervous System after Hands in the Pico progression and distinguish Brain/Mind, Hands, Voice (what a Pico communicates outward), and the transport-neutral fabric those messages travel through. The course defines provider-neutral message semantics — envelope, observation, event, command, delegation, result, presence, discovery, and topic/capability authorization — before naming MQTT or EMQX as candidate transport implementations. See Constructive realization · Nervous system as a governed extension.

See the course descriptor in metadata.yaml for the machine-readable summary (id, level, duration, prerequisites, teaches, produces).
